summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y2→Y3, US Grade 2), skip-counting within 1,000 by 5s, 10s and 100s is a place-value event, not a longer chant: the learner must see WHICH digit rolls when adding 5, 10 or 100, and why a carry happens when crossing a hundred (190→200) or thousand (995→1000) boundary. Core activities drive a live place-value counter from round and ragged starts, with static reference and checking tasks as supports. Non-round starts (5s from 315, 100s from 150/240, 10s from 268) are emphasised so the learner holds the other digits fixed rather than re-rounding to a decade.
misconceptions: Hundred-boundary stall — reaching 190 the child says '191, 192…' or '100-ten', not knowing 200 comes next; the decade/hundred bridge is the classic breakdown point.
'+10 means add a zero' / '+100 means add two zeros' — over-generalised from round numbers, so 268+10 becomes 2680 or 26810.
Treating the count as a longer rote chant and losing track of which digit changes, so skip-counting from a non-round start collapses.
Confusing tens and hundreds steps (counting 240, 250, 260 when asked to skip in 100s) because the difference between which column moves is not yet secure.
Losing the ones digit when skip-counting by 10s or 100s from a ragged start (315→320 instead of 325) because the child re-rounds to a decade.

activities.title: Place-value skip-count playground (drive the carry)
steps: Set a start number — round (e.g. 240) or ragged (e.g. 315, 268) — and choose a step of +5, +10 or +100.
Before tapping, predict aloud the next number and say which digit you think will change.

Tap the step and watch three linked views move together: a thousand grid lights the landed number, a number line draws one equal jump, and place-value columns (H-T-U, with a Th column that appears when you reach 1000) roll the digit or digits that change.
Stop deliberately at 190 and predict 'what comes next in 10s?', then tap +10 and watch ten tens-rods trade for one hundred-flat while the hundreds digit rolls 1→2 and the tens resets to 0.
Repeat the boundary move by counting in 5s up to 995→1000 and describe, in your own words, which columns carried.

Switch to a '10 more / 100 more instantly' challenge: state the answer without counting on by ones, then tap to check which digit rolled (just one digit unless the step crosses a hundred or thousand boundary, e.g. 195 → 205).
activities.insight: Adding 10 rolls the tens digit and adding 100 rolls the hundreds digit; if no boundary is crossed, the other digits stay the same. When a hundred/thousand boundary is crossed (e.g. 190 → 200), the next place up also changes because of regrouping (ten of one place trading for one of the next), not a mysterious jump.

activities.title: Hands-on regrouping with base-ten materials
steps: Build a start number with hundreds flats, tens rods and unit cubes (e.g. 190 as one flat and nine rods).
To add 10, physically add one tens rod; to add 100, add one hundreds flat — and say which digit changed.
At 190, add the tenth rod, then trade ten rods for one hundreds flat to make 200, and say 'the tens rolled to 0 and the hundreds went up by one'.
Skip-count by 100s from 150 using flats, keeping the five tens and nothing in the ones fixed, to reach 250, 350 … 950.
activities.insight: Adding 10 or 100 physically adds a rod or a flat, and crossing a boundary is the concrete act of trading ten rods for one flat — making the digit that changes something the learner can handle and see, not just recite.

activities.title: Annotated thousand-square and place-value reference
steps: Study a thousand grid / linked hundred squares where a 10s count lights one column, a 5s count lights two columns, and a 100s count lights the same position in each hundred square, and name the pattern you see.
Tap a highlighted 100s column to reveal the note 'each step adds one hundred — the hundreds digit changes', and name the H, T, U columns.
Open the flap at the 190→200 join to read how ten tens trade for one hundred.
activities.insight: The 5s/10s/100s patterns fall in predictable places (columns for 5s and 10s, the same position in each hundred square for 100s), and naming the place-value columns helps the learner say which digit each step advances.

activities.title: Checking and diagnostic skip-count tasks
steps: Order a set of 100s cards from 240 and fill blanks in sequences that cross a boundary, e.g. 985, __, 1005.
Answer '100 more than 613' and '10 more than 268', writing the single digit that changed.
Count on in 100s from 150 up to 950; count in 5s from 480 up to 520; count back in 10s from 1000; count on in 100s from 620 and say what happens when the count passes 1000 (920 → 1020).
Explain for each: which digit changed and which stayed the same.
activities.insight: Fluency means changing only the relevant place and crossing hundred and thousand boundaries cleanly, from non-round starts and in both directions.

activities.title: Count-with-me partner rehearsal (spoken practice)
steps: Take turns skip-counting aloud with a counting buddy, alternating each number in a 10s or 100s run.
When the buddy hesitates at 190 in a 10s run, supply the next number (200) and say which digits rolled.
Say each number clearly and, at boundaries, state what carried before moving on.
activities.insight: Rehearsing the count aloud, especially at the deliberate hesitation at a boundary, builds oral fluency and the habit of naming the carry.

checkQuestion: Count on in 100s starting from 150: 150, 250, 350… up to 950. Now count in 5s from 480 up to 520. Then count backwards in 10s from 1000 for a bit. Last, count on by 100s from 620 — what happens at 1000? (Watch counting in 100s from a non-multiple, crossing 500 in 5s, and crossing 1000.)
checkAnswer: 150, 250, …, 950; 480, 485, …, 520 (crossing 500 correctly); 1000, 990, 980…; and 620, 720, 820, 920, 1020 — changing only the relevant place and crossing the thousand boundary cleanly.
